description: The ordered minimal non-TMS consumer journey (single domain, upstream provider): the transcript that proves scenario (a) by construction. Every step of the journey is one data row here, and the Go, TypeScript, and Python suites each execute all 25 rows against the real mounted facade routes, so the journey is executed from shared data rather than narrated. The world is one public base URL `https://mcp.example.com`, a `namespace` route for client namespace `acme`, the route resource and issuer `https://mcp.example.com/acme/mcp`, an upstream provider issuer `https://id.example.com`, the route's protected-resource metadata URL `https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/acme/mcp`, its canonical discovery URL `https://mcp.example.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/acme/mcp` (with `/authorize`, `/token`, and `/register` beneath it), and the stage-global callback `https://mcp.example.com/_oauth/mcp/callback`. Steps 1-11 correspond to MINIMAL_CONSUMER.md. Convention (T1): every authorize step that expects a 302 carries a valid registered client_id and redirect_uri, because errors raised before redirect-URI validation never redirect; only the pre-validation failures (unknown client, unmatched redirect URI) expect 400 with no location. By the same order (DESIGN section 8.1: client -> redirect_uri -> response_type -> S256 PKCE -> state -> resource), every authorize step that expects an error raised later (missing or plain challenge, wrong resource) carries all earlier-validated parameters valid, so the expected error is the only reachable outcome. As built in M3c-1b, steps 9 (`token-refresh`) and 9.1 (`refresh-revoked-handle`) are also executed by the shared `facade-conformance.v1.json` `refresh` rows plus each runtime's concurrency, injected-clock, and capture-and-scan tests: the refresh rotates the handle and returns the upstream access token byte-for-byte, concurrent callers of one handle are single-flighted to the winner's successor tokens, a rotated handle re-presented inside the thirty-second grace window replays the same successor tokens, and a handle revoked by the replayed code of step 7.1 answers the same non-oracle 400 invalid_grant an unknown handle gets. Token-endpoint convention (T2/T3): every authorization_code token step carries the full RFC 6749 section 4.1.3 set (grant_type, code, code_verifier, redirect_uri matching the authorize request, and client_id), so a rejected exchange is the tested fault (replay, verifier mismatch), not a missing-parameter invalid_request. The RFC 8707 `resource` parameter is accepted at the token endpoint but is not required there (DESIGN section 5.3), so the token steps omit it, matching MINIMAL_CONSUMER.md step 7. Negative assertions pinned across the journey: no upstream authorization code in any client-visible response; no upstream refresh token in any client-visible response; no id_token in any client-visible response; the access_token is byte-identical to the upstream-minted token; a token for one route is refused at another route; and handler_invocations is 0 on every denied transport step. A row's `stage` names the harness action and the remaining fields are the closed row vocabulary each runtime's single dispatcher understands; a case whose `group` is not `journey` is rejected rather than silently ignored.

contract.name: Minimal non-TMS consumer journey (single domain, upstream provider)
contract.notes: The ordered transcript that proves scenario (a) by construction. HTTP-shaped so M1-M3 can lift each step into a tier:facade single-envelope fixture. Steps 1-11 correspond to MINIMAL_CONSUMER.md. Convention (T1): every authorize step that expects a 302 carries a valid registered client_id and redirect_uri, because errors raised before redirect-URI validation never redirect; only the pre-validation failures (unknown client, unmatched redirect URI) expect 400 with no location. By the same order (DESIGN §8.1: client -> redirect_uri -> response_type -> S256 PKCE -> state -> resource), every authorize step that expects an error raised later (missing or plain challenge, wrong resource) carries all earlier-validated parameters valid — response_type and, unless the step is itself testing it, S256 code_challenge/code_challenge_method — so the expected error is the only reachable outcome. As built in M3c-1b, steps 9 (`token-refresh`) and 9.1 (`refresh-revoked-handle`) are EXECUTED in Go, TypeScript, and Python as the shared `facade-conformance.v1.json` `refresh` rows plus each runtime's concurrency, injected-clock, and capture-and-scan tests: the refresh rotates the handle and returns the upstream access token byte-for-byte, concurrent callers of one handle are single-flighted to the winner's successor tokens, a rotated handle re-presented inside the thirty-second grace window replays the same successor tokens, and a handle revoked by the replayed code of step 7.1 answers the same non-oracle 400 invalid_grant an unknown handle gets. Token-endpoint convention (T2/T3): every authorization_code token step carries the full RFC 6749 §4.1.3 set — grant_type, code, code_verifier, redirect_uri (matching the authorize request), and client_id — so a rejected exchange is the tested fault (replay, verifier mismatch), not a missing-parameter invalid_request. The RFC 8707 `resource` parameter is accepted at the token endpoint but is not required there (DESIGN §5.3 says resource is accepted at authorize and token, and the facade code already binds the route), so the token steps above omit it — matching MINIMAL_CONSUMER.md step 7.

negative_assertions: no upstream authorization code in any client-visible response
no upstream refresh token in any client-visible response
no id_token in any client-visible response
access_token is byte-identical to the upstream-minted token
a token for one route is refused at another route
handler_invocations == 0 on every denied transport step

cases.reason: A credential-free JSON-RPC POST to the transport is refused with the RFC 9728 challenge that names the route's protected-resource metadata, and the MCP handler never runs.
The route's RFC 9728 document names the route resource and the route as its own authorization server, and is uncacheable.

The routed RFC 8414 document advertises the route issuer and the route's own endpoints, the upstream key set that signs the access tokens the route hands clients, and S256 as the only PKCE method; registration_endpoint is advertised because the front channel mounts the register route. It also advertises RFC 9207 `iss` support, because the front channel sends the route issuer as `iss` on the client callback, the same `iss` step 6 pins on the redirect.
A public client registers (RFC 7591) with a server-assigned id bound to the advertising route, and the response is uncacheable.
An http non-loopback redirect URI is refused at registration.
The eleventh registration attempt inside one rate-limit window is refused with a retry hint.

The browser is sent to the upstream authorize endpoint with the facade's own client, callback, S256 challenge, resource, and a freshly minted upstream state distinct from the client's state; the transaction is recorded single-use.
An unknown client is refused before redirect-URI validation, so the response is a 400 error page with no location.
Error page, never a redirect: an unmatched redirect URI is refused pre-redirect (open-redirect defense).
code_challenge required: the redirect URI and response_type are already validated, so the refusal is a redirect carrying invalid_request.
S256 required; plain refused. Every earlier-validated parameter is valid, so invalid_request is the only reachable outcome.

resource must equal the route resource; every earlier-validated parameter (client, redirect URI, response_type, S256 PKCE, state) is valid, so under the DESIGN section 8.1 validation order this error is the only reachable outcome.

The upstream return is completed into a facade code plus the client's own state and the route issuer; the redirect carries no upstream code, refresh token, or id_token, and the MCP handler never runs.

The callback presents a facade-minted (hence valid) upstream state AND a facade-minted (hence exchangeable) upstream code, so the state check passes and the upstream exchange would succeed (302 with a broker record) for an implementation that never verifies the upstream RFC 9207 iss; a compliant implementation verifies iss before consuming the transaction or exchanging the code (DESIGN section 8.2), so the mismatch is the only reachable rejection and nothing is consumed; the callback's own 400 is furthermore distinguishable from an upstream-exchange failure (502 upstream_error), so the pin does not rest on the exchange mapping.
Already completed, restart sign-in: the transaction store burned the state on first consume, so a replay is terminal and never re-exchanges.

The upstream state was never minted by the facade, so it keys no transaction (callback CSRF / session-swap defense, T10); an implementation that skipped the state check would accept the forged state and reach the upstream exchange, whose failure maps to 502 upstream_error rather than the pinned 400, so removing the control changes the expected result.

The callback presents a facade-minted (hence valid) upstream state and a facade-minted (hence exchangeable) upstream code but omits the upstream RFC 9207 iss parameter; a compliant implementation rejects an absent iss before consuming the transaction or exchanging the code (DESIGN section 8.2), so the callback lands in the same (400, no Location) class as an iss mismatch, nothing is consumed, and no upstream exchange is attempted; an implementation that treated an absent iss as unpinned would reach the exchange (or mint a broker record) and change the pinned result.
The code exchange returns the upstream access token byte-for-byte and an opaque framework refresh handle, never the upstream refresh token or an id_token; the MCP handler never runs.

The required parameter set is complete (grant_type, code, code_verifier, redirect_uri matching step 5, client_id), so the fault is the replay and invalid_grant is reachable; the replay revokes the broker record the code minted.
The required parameter set is complete, so the fault is the S256 verifier mismatch and invalid_grant is reachable.
The access token the code exchange handed the client is accepted at the transport and the MCP handler runs exactly once.
A token minted for another route is refused at this route without invoking the MCP handler.

The refresh rotates the handle, returns the upstream access token byte-for-byte, and leaks no upstream refresh material or id_token. Concurrent callers of one handle are single-flighted to the winner's successor tokens, and a rotated handle re-presented inside the thirty-second grace window replays the same successor tokens; both are pinned by the shared facade-conformance.v1.json refresh rows and each runtime's concurrency and injected-clock tests.
A handle revoked by the replayed code of step 7.1 answers the same non-oracle invalid_grant an unknown handle gets.
An expired bearer token is refused with the same RFC 9728 challenge a credential-free request gets, and the MCP handler never runs.
A token missing mcp:tools is refused with the RFC 6750 insufficient_scope challenge naming the route-derived remediation scope, and the MCP handler never runs.
